</t>Under California law, the jury will be instructed to compensate our client for what could be decades of past and future noneconomic damages in the form of past and future physical pain, mental suffering, loss of enjoyment of life, disfigurement, physical impairment, inconvenience, grief, anxiety, humiliation, indignity, embarrassment, and emotional distress suffered due to this accident. CACI 3905A; Capelouto v. Kaiser Foundation Hospitals (1972) 7 Cal. 3d 889, 892-893. As the foregoing medical summary has outlined, [Clientname] has most certainly experienced many [if not all] of these noneconomic damages in a painfully significant and life-altering way.

[PainAndSuffringSection]

                    

Monetary Past Non-Economic Damages Calculations

</t>Personal pain and suffering can be difficult to quantify into a dollar value, as are the unavoidable burdens and inconveniences and associated anxiety and frustration one suffers when forced into becoming a patient and litigant owing to the wanton inattentiveness of a negligent driver. And our client is no exception. Based on the above description of the pain, suffering, and loss of enjoyment of life, [Clientname] is entitled to significant compensation for past non-economic damages.

</t>It has been [monthsDifference] months since this accident occurred on [AccidentDate]. Given the significant disruption [he/she] experienced to [his/her] life through the present with the pain, suffering, limitation, and extensive medical treatment of the past [monthsDifference] months, it would not be unreasonable for a jury to award [Clientname] [PastMonthlyPainAmount] per month in past pain and suffering ([perDayPasNonEconomicDamagesFinalAmount] per day). Accordingly, [Clientname] is entitled to at least $[pastNonEconomicDamages] in past non-economic damages through the present.

   

Monetary Future Non-Economic Damages Calculations

</t>As outlined above, our client remains in significant pain from this accident, is still hampered by various profound limitations in [his/her] physical life and must now drastically curtail [his/her] personal aspirations to accommodate the potential risk of exacerbation to [his/her] injuries. California Civil Jury Instruction CACI 3905A states:

No fixed standard exists for deciding the amount of these noneconomic damages. You must use your judgment to decide a reasonable amount based on the evidence and your common sense. To recover for future pain and suffering, [Clientname] must prove that [he/she] is reasonably certain to suffer that harm. For future pain and suffering, determine the amount in current dollars paid at the time of judgment that will compensate [his/her] for future pain and suffering.

</t>Juries can have difficulty in measuring pain and suffering awards into the future. Our courts have recognized that a “per diem” approach may be the easiest form of calculation in many circumstances:﻿

Every case which has considered the issue before us has emphasized the difficulty faced by a jury in attempting to measure in monetary terms compensation for injuries as subjective as pain, humiliation and embarrassment. The cases abound in broad statements such as that the matter is entrusted to the impartial conscience and judgment of jurors who may be expected to act reasonably, intelligently and in harmony with the evidence, and that they are to award fair and reasonable compensation and be guided by their observation, experience and sense of fairness and right. These homilies provide little assistance to the jury.

﻿Under some circumstances, the concept of pain and suffering may become more meaningful when it is measured in short periods of time than over a span of many years, perhaps into infinity. The worth of pain over a period of decades is often more difficult to grasp as a concept of reality than is the same experience limited to a day, a week or a month. It is this very consideration which underlies much of the controversy over the issue before us. The fact that the per diem argument provides a more explicit comprehension and humanization of the plaintiff's predicament to lay jurors makes this approach an effective tool in the hands of his attorney. Beagle v. Vasold (1966) 65 Cal.2d 166, 172.

</t>Here, the jury will be instructed to compensate our client for what could be decades of future pain and suffering. Based on the CACI government tables of life expectancy, at only [Age] years old, [Clientname] has an actual life expectancy of [lifeExpectancyAge] more years wherein [he/she] would live with significant ongoing daily pain.

</t>The jury will also be instructed that the “per diem” (i.e. per day or per year) approach is one manner they may use to calculate our client’s monetary non-economic damages over the remaining [lifeExpectancyAge] years of [his/her] life. Accordingly, even if a jury only awarded [Clientname] [FutureYearlyPainAmount] in future pain and suffering per year (less than $[perDayAmountForFutureNonEconomicDamages] per day), [he/she] would be entitled to [postNonEconomicsDamagesFinalAmount] in future noneconomic damages.
